cadet.name: The Four Pillars Checklist
cadet.note: End of month one. Score yourself out of ten first; your leader signs once you have done it independently in the field.

items.text: Read a customer as red, amber or green before speaking, and adjust the approach to match
Match and mirror pace and body language without it being noticeable
Hold control with someone resistant at the start, and still get to a presentation
Hold eye contact all the way through the close without dropping it
Vary volume, pace and inflection deliberately inside one presentation
Use a pause to create weight instead of filling the silence
Use all four closes across a week — at least once each
Pre-empt a common objection, then handle three others through to a re-close
Use each of the five influences deliberately in a live pitch
Hold your attitude after a rejected close and move straight to the next person
Track your own T&M card for a full week, find your limiting factor from it, and work that one skill
Explain the 8 successful business habits and say honestly where you're weakest in it

captain.name: The 4-Week New Leader Challenge
captain.note: Complete each milestone, get your mentor to sign off, and aim to complete all 20 within your first 4 weeks of Leadership.

items.text: Ring the bell on a solo shift (city)
Hit 8+ sales in a single day
Ring the bell on a Saturday or Sunday shift
Hit a new weekly sales PB
Play “linchpin” role on a business trip
Organise and run a morning topic in Primetime
Submit 1 week's worth of T&M cards
Submit weekly wrap and goals 4 weeks consecutively
1-on-1 SWOT analysis with MD/TM
1-on-1 monthly AUTOP review with mentor
Submit 4-week quadrant goals to MD/TM
Shadow 10-day training plan with mentor
Complete Sales Fundamentals on Growth Academy (inc. notes)
Submit a personal referral
40 sales over a 2-week period
$2,400 retail, 60 memberships and 20 credit cards for the campaign
4-day bell streak in the city
30% CC's and 15 TRPH back-to-back weeks
2 sales after 5pm in the city
Secure a spot on a Wednesday Workshop or Rising Star event

coach.name: The Coach Checklist
coach.note: Your mentor signs each line when it is a habit — not the first time you manage it. Start the two long ones first.

items.text: Place yourself honestly on the five levels and review it with your mentor
Name which of the eight gaps is holding you back, and what you're doing about it
Coach the same skill to two people in different matrix zones, using a different approach for each
Set a day up with a goal and a focus for every person — including yours
Close a day off with a full debrief on every person you had out
Run a coaching call under ten minutes that ends on a specific, checkable ask
Design and run a training topic
Complete a 10 day training plan with a new start
Place every person on your team on the matrix, and say what each one needs next
Diagnose two people from their numbers alone, before you speak to them
Plan and submit a training plan for your team
Analyse your weekly KPI and reject report with your mentor
Create a team profile
Plan, set up and close off a sales day
Run a shift where you hand over between two people and both finish to their goal
Plan, run and debrief a business trip
Submit and run a team meeting
Submit a 12 week business plan

sections.title: The Two Long Ones — Start These First

items.text: Take a new start from their first day through to working independently — and keep them
Have someone you trained take a new start of their own

mentor.name: The Mentor Checklist
mentor.note: Eighteen things. Your mentor signs each one when it is a habit. Three take months — start those in week one.

items.text: Name your two weakest battery habits, and show your mentor what changed over a fortnight
Go a full week answering questions with questions — then tell your mentor what happened
Explain the core equation to your mentor using your own family tree
Score your whole team against the ten markers, revise it a month later, and talk through what changed
Rate yourself against the standard and review your two lowest with your mentor
Run the vehicle conversation with someone on your team, start to finish
Hand a job over using the coaching flywheel — you do it, together, they do it
Coach one of your leaders on their coaching
Talk your mentor through a decision you made using best case, worst case, most likely
Develop a leader on one of your leaders' teams
Walk your mentor through your placement plan — where the next two leaders go, and who replaces them
Run a one-on-one with every one of your leaders inside the same month
Plan and run a leaders' workshop — a real problem, ending in a decision
Do the weekly family tree pass four weeks straight
Rate yourself on the symbiotic relationship and compare with your mentor's score
Run your mentor's team meeting
Complete the impact player self-assessment and compare scores with your mentor
Hold a team of four leaders for a full month

manager.name: The Manager Checklist
manager.note: Nineteen things. Your mentor signs each one when it is a habit. Four take months — start those first.

items.text: Maintain a written personal growth plan and review it with your mentor
Go a full month where your own field days are booked before anything else
Run each tier meeting you're responsible for, anchored to its training book
Deliver an opportunity meeting — the vision and the why behind the goals
Hand a tier meeting over to one of your leaders and debrief them on it
Run your full weekly cadence for four weeks straight without dropping one
Have every leader explain the bonus structure back to you, correctly
Run an expectations meeting and document it
Have a critical conversation within a week of the behaviour, not a month
Complete a SWOT and 12 week game plan with a developing leader
Coach one of your leaders through a hard conversation of their own
Map your family tree and identify where the depth gaps are
Talk your mentor through a live placement decision and why you made it
Know your group's average tenure and what's moved it in the last quarter
Present your group scoreboard against benchmarks at a monthly review
Maintain current emerging leader and emerging core lists, revised monthly
Build and submit a 12 week business plan for your group

sections.title: The Long Ones — Start These First

items.text: Develop a second-generation leader — a leader on one of your leaders' teams
Hold a group of four or more leaders for a full quarter

questions.q: SEEC is the energy you bring before you say a word. What do the four letters stand for?
o: Smile, Eye Contact, Enthusiasm, Confidence
Speed, Energy, Engagement, Control
Smile, Empathy, Excitement, Closing
Stance, Eyes, Enthusiasm, Cadence
questions.w: Smile, Eye Contact, Enthusiasm, Confidence — the energy you carry into every interaction before a word is spoken.

questions.q: In Distance Theory, what happens at 3 metres — the Power Zone?
o: Assumptive body language, super confident — this is where the stop happens
Wave, smile and make eye contact to set the tone early
Greet them with a hook and keep moving toward them
Start the FORM questions to warm them up
questions.w: 10m is the wave zone, 6m is the hook ("Before you run..."), 3m is the Power Zone ("Just quickly...") — where the stop happens.

questions.q: You read a customer as a red light. What is the right approach?
o: Go direct — short responses, straight to the pitch, rapport only after commitment
Slow down and spend more time on rapport
Open up with lots of questions and pitch big
Use jokes to break the ice before you pitch
questions.w: Red light means cautious and closed. Match their speed, go straight to the pitch and close, and build rapport only after commitment.

questions.q: In the FORM rapport guide, what does the 'M' stand for — and why does it matter?
o: Motivation — it reveals the hot button you tie back to the cause
Money — it tells you how much to ask for
Mindset — it shows whether they are a red or green light
Mood — it tells you when to close
questions.w: Family, Occupation, Recreation, Motivation. Motivation reveals what the customer values, which is where you find the hot button.

questions.q: ACE is what makes the Law of Averages work. What are the three?
o: Attitude, Consistency, Exposure
Attitude, Confidence, Energy
Action, Commitment, Effort
Awareness, Control, Engagement
questions.w: Attitude — approach every person as a sale. Consistency — stick to your process. Exposure — see as many people as possible.

questions.q: There are five types of close. Which one is used all the way through the presentation rather than at the commitment?
o: The trial close
The assumptive close
The alternative close
The silent close
questions.w: The trial close ("Makes sense, right?") is used throughout, like a tie-down or yes question. The other four are the closes at the commitment.

questions.q: The five steps of the pitch run Intro, Short Story, Presentation, Commitment… what is the last step?
o: Consolidation — leave the client feeling great about their decision
Rapport — build a five-minute friend
Trial close — check they are still with you
Objection handling — clear any doubts
questions.w: Intro → Short Story → Presentation → Commitment → Consolidation. Consolidation confirms details, explains what happens next and re-enforces the decision.

questions.q: Sales Influences follow ABOUT. What does the U stand for?
o: Urgency — guiding them decisively toward a clear yes or no
Understanding — listening for their hot button
Upselling — moving them to a bigger package
Usefulness — showing what the product does
questions.w: Assuredness, Benefits, Opportunity, Urgency, Trends. Urgency does not mean rushing — it means guiding them toward a decision now.

questions.q: A customer raises an objection. Which model do you use?
o: LREC — Listen, Relate, Educate, Close
GRASP — Get around the right people, Responsibility, Attitude, Systems, Profit
SEEC — Smile, Eye contact, Enthusiasm, Confidence
IOPM — Intro, Observe, Practice, Master
questions.w: Great salespeople do not argue objections — they Listen, Relate, Educate and Close.

questions.q: Your week: 3.2 stops an hour, 72% stops to presentations, 70% presentations to close, 22% close to sale. In your first month, what is your limiting factor?
o: Stops to presentations
Stops per hour
Presentations to close
Close to sale
questions.w: Read down the funnel. Stops are on the 3+ mark for your first month, so the first metric below benchmark is stops to presentations (80%). Fix that one and everything below it lifts.

questions.q: The Four Pillars Checklist you sign at the end of month one covers which four pillars?
o: First Impressions, Communication, Negotiation, Mindset
Stops, Presentations, Closes, Sales
Attitude, Consistency, Exposure, Goals
Health, Relationships, Business, Finances
questions.w: First Impressions, Communication, Negotiation and Mindset — three skills each, signed once you have done them independently in the field.

questions.q: Through your first month, 3+ stops an hour is the mark. What becomes the mark from the end of month one?
o: 3.5 stops an hour
3 stops an hour still
4 stops an hour
5 stops an hour
questions.w: Through your first month, 3+ stops an hour is the mark — from the end of month one, 3.5 becomes the new mark.

questions.q: Quality is "the number behind the numbers". What two things come out of quality?
o: A long-term customer and a low reject rate
A higher $ average and more credit cards
More stops and more presentations
A faster pitch and more sales per hour
questions.w: The educated customer stays. If they could not explain it back, it was not a sale — it was a signature.

questions.q: In GRASP, G + R + A + S = Profit. What does the A stand for?
o: Attitude
Action
Awareness
Accountability
questions.w: Get around the right people, Responsibility, Attitude, Systems = Profit.

questions.q: On the 5 Phases of Leadership, Months 2–3 — where a new leader is — is focused on…
o: Learning to manage yourself
Guide and train new starts
Lead and coach performance
Mentor and manage others
questions.w: Month 1 introduction to sales performance, Months 2–3 learning to manage yourself, Months 3–6 guide and train new starts, Months 6–12 lead and coach performance, Months 12–24 mentor and manage others.

questions.q: Balancing volume and value is about which transition?
o: From personal performance to training performance
From chasing volume to chasing bigger sales
From following systems to trusting instinct
From field work to office work
questions.w: Your standard becomes the team standard — the shift is from personal performance to training performance.

questions.q: The 10-day training plan follows the IOPM model. What is it?
o: Intro, Observe, Practice, Master
Introduce, Optimise, Perform, Measure
Instruct, Observe, Praise, Move on
Inform, Order, Practise, Manage
questions.w: Intro → Observe → Practice → Master. New skills are modelled before they are tried.

questions.q: One objective of a training plan is that it…
o: Sets an expectation of speed of learning and holds coach and student accountable
Guarantees the new start a sale by Day 10
Removes the need for field training later
Lets a confident new start skip the reviews
questions.w: It utilises your network, gives new mentors a framework, and sets the speed of learning while holding both coach and student accountable.

questions.q: When should new information be introduced to a new start?
o: Only outside of field hours — and modelled before they try it
Whenever a teachable moment appears mid-shift
During the first pitch of the morning
At the customer's door, for realism
questions.w: Only introduce new information outside of field hours, model new skills first, and cater for auditory, visual and kinaesthetic learners.

questions.q: In the 4 Layers of Field Feedback, what does 'Ask Permission' mean?
o: Bring them into the learning before coaching
Get sign-off from your manager before giving feedback
Ask the customer before you step in
Check they want to pitch solo
questions.w: Laugh / Acknowledge, Ask Permission, Accept Responsibility, Ring the Bell. Ask Permission brings them into the learning before you coach.

questions.q: Across a new start's ten days, what is each week built around?
o: Week one — getting stops. Week two — closing the sale.
Week one — product knowledge. Week two — the iPad process.
Week one — closing. Week two — objection handling.
Week one — goals. Week two — numbers.
questions.w: Days 1–5 are about getting stops, with a review at Day 5. Days 6–10 are about closing the sale, with a sign-off at Day 10, then the Level Up in week three.

questions.q: The coaching cycle in The Captain runs in which order?
o: Deliver the topic → practice run → demonstrate on the field → review → re-enforce
Demonstrate → deliver the topic → review → practice run
Review → deliver the topic → re-enforce → demonstrate
Practice run → review → deliver the topic → demonstrate
questions.w: Deliver the topic, practise it before the field, demonstrate it on the field, review their performance, then re-enforce the lesson.

questions.q: How many milestones are in the New Leader Challenge, and what is the target?
o: 20 milestones, aiming to complete them all within your first 4 weeks
12 milestones within your first 8 weeks
20 milestones within your first 8 weeks
31 milestones within your first 3 months
questions.w: The 4-Week New Leader Challenge — 20 milestones, each signed off by your mentor.

questions.q: In the New Leader road map, 'Leadership performance review' covers…
o: The AUTOP monthly review and how to monitor team results
Sitting an HR-style appraisal with the owner
Reviewing the owner's performance
Your personal sales average for the quarter
questions.w: Leadership performance review — the AUTOP monthly review, monitoring team results and current KPIs against benchmark.

questions.q: 'Becoming a business partner' in the road map is about…
o: Understanding GRASP and becoming a core member of the team
Buying into the business financially
Running your own office within a year
Recruiting your first new start
questions.w: Becoming a business partner — understanding GRASP and becoming a core member of the team.

questions.q: Quadrant goals balance four areas. Which four?
o: Health, Relationship, Business, Finance
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic
Stops, Presentations, Closes, Sales
Daily, Weekly, Monthly, Yearly
questions.w: Quadrant goals cover health, relationship, business and finance — how you find your why. S.M.A.R.T. is the method, not the quadrants.

questions.q: "The speed of the leader is…"
o: …the speed of the team
…the speed of the sale
…set by the owner
…measured in stops per hour
questions.w: The speed of the leader is the speed of the team. Great leaders make sales fun and look easy.

questions.q: What triggers the Performing Leader meeting?
o: Consistent results in the field
A set number of weeks as a leader
Passing the Welcome to Leadership review
Recruiting your first new start
questions.w: It is triggered by consistent field results — you have proven you can perform, so the focus moves to building the momentum of a team.

questions.q: What is a limiting factor?
o: The one KPI holding everything else back
The KPI you are already best at
A cap the office sets on each rep
The weakest person on your team
questions.w: Fix that one thing and all the others improve. Coaching everything at once leads to confusion, not growth.

questions.q: Running a limiting-factor session, once you find the first metric below benchmark you…
o: Find that topic in the Sales Skills section and run a focused impact before the next field day
Coach every metric that is below benchmark at once
Compare them to the best rep in the office
Wait another week to see if it fixes itself
questions.w: Open AUTOP, filter the period, compare each KPI to benchmark, find the first one below — that is the constraint — then run a focused impact on it.

questions.q: On the KPI Cheat Sheet, what is the Stops → Presentations benchmark?
questions.w: Stops → Presentations 80%, Presentations → Close 75%, Close → Sale 30%, $ Average $40, CC% 30%.

questions.q: Submit in AUTOP is the #1 daily habit. How long should it take?
o: Less than 15 seconds
Under 5 minutes
Around 15 minutes
Around half an hour
questions.w: End of day — select campaign, enter numbers, less than 15 seconds. If it is too complicated, your team will not use it.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the reasons people join our business?
o: Job security
Opportunity
Belief
Earning potential
questions.w: People join for Opportunity, Belief, Relationships, Fun and Earning Potential — knowing which helps you speak to what matters to them from Day 1.

questions.q: Your new start is Under Confident. Best approach?
o: Small targets within each skill, goals around activity not results
Push them to close the biggest sale they can
Compare their numbers with the top rep
Leave them to build it up on their own
questions.w: Set small targets within each skill, keep it simple, set goals around activity not results, and inspire them with progress over outcomes.

questions.q: Your new start is an Overthinker / Sceptical. Best approach?
o: Learn their long-term motivation, introduce relatable people, and don't over-coach
Give them lots of new skills quickly
Focus only on their results
Direct every move they make tightly
questions.w: They are often influenced by people rather than position. Show assuredness in the field and about the opportunity.

questions.q: In Situational Leadership, an advanced performer needs which style?
o: Delegating
Directing
Coaching
Supporting
questions.w: Beginner — Direct. Intermediate — Coaching. Developing — Supporting. Advanced — Delegating.

questions.q: How To Build A Topic has four stages. Which stage do most topics skip?
o: Skill Practice — letting them do it
Introduction — gaining attention
Content — the key points
Applying & Adapting — making it land
questions.w: Most topics stop after content. Skill practice is the stage that turns information into ability — all four stages, every time.

questions.q: In the end of day debrief, you…
o: Ask how they felt, debrief positives first, then agree one coaching objective
Read out the numbers and send everyone home
Start with what went wrong while it is fresh
Give them a list of everything to fix
questions.w: Ask how they felt, positives first then challenges, go through paperwork and KPIs, agree one coaching objective, finish on a positive.

questions.q: The skills a new start needs, just out of reach, sit in which zone?
o: The learning zone
The comfort zone
The panic zone
The power zone
questions.w: Panic zone — anxious and cannot learn. Comfort zone — stopped learning. Learning zone — the skills just out of reach.

questions.q: Taking a new start into the field is…
o: A privilege, not a right — earned by being reliable and consistent in your own sales
A right once you are promoted to leader
Allocated by roster to every leader equally
Something you do once you have ten sales a day
questions.w: Earning the right: consistent sales performance, a genuine desire to develop others, the right image, and competence explaining the business end to end.

questions.q: On the five levels of leadership, where does The Coach live?
o: Between Level Three (Production) and Level Four (People Development)
Between Level One (Position) and Level Two (Permission)
At Level Five (Pinnacle)
At Level One — the new title
questions.w: You have proven you can produce. This book is the shift to being measured by what other people produce.

questions.q: Why do most people stop at Level Three — Production?
o: It feels good — the recognition is immediate and the feedback same-day
The business does not reward developers
They run out of people to train
Level Four needs a promotion first
questions.w: Good leaders build more producers. Great leaders build more leaders. Most stay excellent producers and cap out.

questions.q: Someone says "I don't feel like doing it." Which of the eight gaps are they in?
o: The Inspiration Gap — a habit problem, because the feeling follows the action
The Knowledge Gap — they need more information
The Timing Gap — wait for a better week
The Comparison Gap — they compare themselves to others
questions.w: You cannot fix an inspiration gap with more information. Work out which gap someone is in before you decide what to do.

questions.q: Captain, don't coach. Before giving feedback, what do you ask yourself?
o: Am I telling here, or showing? Could I show this instead?
Is this the most important thing to fix today?
Will they take this well?
Should my manager say this instead?
questions.w: People copy what they see far more reliably than they follow what they are told.

questions.q: A great setup leaves every person with which two things?
o: A goal — a number for today — and a focus — one skill
A site and a start time
A list of three skills and a target
A partner and a sales script
questions.w: A goal and a focus for everyone — including you. Decrease anxiety, increase certainty.

questions.q: Feedback about someone's attitude or effort should be given…
o: In private — never in front of others
On the spot, while it is fresh
In the team meeting so everyone learns
In the group chat
questions.w: Praise in public, correct in private, and never correct while you are annoyed.

questions.q: In the debrief — wins, misses, future focus — who goes first?
o: They do, on all three — then you add
You do, so they know what you saw
The best performer on the team
Whoever had the worst day
questions.w: They will usually name the miss themselves, and something they identify sticks in a way something they are told never does.

questions.q: On the Coaching Matrix, which is the biggest zone?
o: Coaching — moderate skill, moderate motivation
Empowering — high skill, high motivation
Directing — low skill, low motivation
Enthusiastic — low skill, high motivation
questions.w: Most of your team, most of the time. If most of your team is in Directing or Counselling, the problem is not the individuals.

questions.q: A previously strong performer has gone flat — the skill is there, the output has dropped. Which zone?
o: Counselling — investigate, don't coach the skill
Enthusiastic — tell, show, show, tell
Directing — specific how, what and when
Empowering — give them more ownership
questions.w: High skill, low motivation. Something motivational or attitudinal has shifted — address it early, before it becomes cultural.

questions.q: Someone's sales are low. Where do you look first?
o: Left to right — fix the first broken number, starting with stops
Their closing technique
Their $ average
Their objection handling
questions.w: A low sales figure is almost never a closing problem. Coaching the close when the stops are down is the most common wasted conversation.

questions.q: Strategic versus tactical coaching:
o: Strategic — how they approach the market and customer. Tactical — selling skills in an actual conversation.
Strategic — for new starts. Tactical — for leaders.
Strategic — in the office. Tactical — on the phone.
Strategic — long sessions. Tactical — short ones.
questions.w: Strategic works away from the moment, in a setup or a drive. Tactical works in the moment and immediately after.

questions.q: When should you NOT reach for coaching?
o: When someone is chronically late or has stopped caring
When they are new to the job
When they had a big day yesterday
When the site is quiet
questions.w: Coaching does not solve everything. Assess two things — can they do it, and do they want to.

questions.q: The 3/3/3 framework covers which three horizons?
o: 3 Years, 3 Months, 3 Weeks
3 Days, 3 Weeks, 3 Months
3 Months, 3 Quarters, 3 Years
3 Hours, 3 Days, 3 Weeks
questions.w: The big picture, the 12-week map, and daily accountability. People buy into the leader before they buy into the vision.

questions.q: What does GOMO stand for?
o: Going through the motions
Growth of my output
Getting on and moving on
Goals over mindset obstacles
questions.w: GOMO is stagnation and plateau. Re-assess your goals and re-establish your focus to get your MOJO back.

questions.q: At four or more leaders, what replaces holding everyone in your head?
o: Rhythm and structure — meetings that happen on schedule and a tree you can read on paper
Being available to everyone, all the time
Solving the hard problems personally
Informal check-ins whenever you notice something
questions.w: Being available becomes a bottleneck and solving problems personally stops leaders solving their own. The cadence is the product.

questions.q: What is the signal you have made the shift from very senior mentor to manager?
o: Something goes wrong two levels below you and is solved before you hear about it
Your own sales stay the highest in the group
Every problem comes to you first
You run every morning meeting yourself
questions.w: Then your leader tells you afterwards, unprompted, what they did and why. Systems run the business — the manager runs the systems.

questions.q: Where should a new person be placed?
o: On a developing leader's team, one at a time — not your strongest leader, and not you
On your strongest leader, so they are looked after
On your own team until they are settled
With whichever leader has the fewest people
questions.w: Build around your leaders, not through them. You carry more of the coaching early and the split moves toward the leader over the following months.

questions.q: Why does a manager stay in the field?
o: Credibility, first-generation development, and a true read on the group
Because the group needs their sales to hit target
Because leaders cannot run a site without them
Only to cover for people who are away
questions.w: Once you are out of the field, your picture comes from what you are told and leaders start managing your perception. Book your own field days first.

questions.q: The three layers of meetings answer three questions. Which layer answers "Who is growing?"
o: Development — tier meetings, one-on-ones, networking calls
Daily — Primetime, morning meeting, impact topic
Direction — opportunity meeting, expectations resets, SWOT
Monthly — the scoreboard review
questions.w: Daily: how are we going? Development: who is growing? Direction: where are we going? Development is the most commonly dropped layer.

questions.q: What makes a tier meeting a tier meeting rather than a catch-up?
o: It is anchored to a training book and runs a section of it
It runs for at least an hour
Every level attends together
It is held only when someone is struggling
questions.w: If a meeting cannot name the section it is running, it is a catch-up with a title. Everyone leaves with one thing, written down, with a date.

questions.q: The opportunity meeting is about…
o: The vision and the why behind the goals — where the organisation is going
The day's sales target
Recruitment numbers for the month
Fixing a drop in results
questions.w: Run it on a schedule — usually monthly — not when recruitment feels slow, or it reads as a pitch.

questions.q: Culture is best described as…
o: The standards that hold on an ordinary Tuesday when nobody senior is watching
The team nights and celebrations
What the owner says at the morning meeting
The office rules written on the wall
questions.w: Every standard is set by what gets tolerated rather than what gets said. Standards slip by tolerance, never by decision.

questions.q: People rarely leave because the next step was too hard. They leave because…
o: They couldn't see one, or the one they could see kept moving
The pay was too low
Their leader was too strict
The field was too hard
questions.w: People don't leave hard next steps — they leave invisible ones. Each book states what its level is for and carries a checklist.

questions.q: A critical conversation should happen…
o: Within a week of the behaviour, not a month
At the next quarterly review
Only once it has happened three times
In front of the team so everyone learns
questions.w: Have a critical conversation within a week of the behaviour, not a month — and coach your leaders through their own rather than having them for them.

questions.q: A family tree is different from an org chart because it shows…
o: Who developed whom
Who reports to whom
Who has the highest sales
Who has been there longest
questions.w: A tree with layers is a business — a tree without them is a team with a good salesperson at the top.

questions.q: Why build depth above the promotion criteria?
o: Criteria describe when someone is ready, not when a structure is stable
Because the criteria are only a guide
To get promoted faster
So you can skip the 12 week plan
questions.w: If the criteria say two, the groups that hold together build three — so a departure leaves you above the line rather than scrambling back to it.

questions.q: Speed to leadership is best understood as…
o: A systems measure — it tests whether your training works end to end
A measure of one exceptional individual
How quickly the owner promotes people
The number of leaders in the office
questions.w: One leader is a result — a leader's leader is a system.

questions.q: The shift from hero to hero maker means you are measured by…
o: What the people around you become
What you produce personally
How many people you recruit
How quickly you solve problems
questions.w: The hero gets their name on the result. The hero maker gets other people's names on results.

questions.q: Someone you developed starts developing their own people. On Add, Multiply, Exponential, that is…
o: Exponential — it keeps going without you
Addition — you get better
Multiplication — everyone you develop lifts
Production — your results improve
questions.w: Yourself is addition, others is multiplication, others developing others is exponential.

questions.q: The 80 / 20 shift at Level Four means roughly…
o: 80% of your time on other people, 20% on your own productivity
80% selling, 20% coaching
80% recruiting, 20% training
100% developing leaders, no selling
questions.w: Not a target for next week — the direction of travel.

questions.q: Solving every problem your team brings you is the helpful leader trap. It raises…
o: House cats — loyal, and unable to operate without you
Strays — independent problem solvers
Core people ready to lead
High rollers who out-sell you
questions.w: Instead of answering, ask: What do you think we should do? Where have you got to? Run me through your thinking.

questions.q: The weekly question for measuring your multiplication is…
o: Who is more capable this week than last week — because of me?
How many sales did my team make this week?
Who had the best numbers on my tree?
How many calls did I take this week?
questions.w: If you cannot answer it two weeks running, you are managing, not mentoring.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the ten that charge your battery?
o: Be less reachable
Answer every call straight away
Work through the weekend
Cut back on sleep in a big week
questions.w: Sleep, bedtime, prioritising, a place to work, vices, be less reachable, information diet, walk, journal, diet and exercise.

questions.q: According to the core equation, scale is directly proportional to…
o: Your number of core people
The hours you put in
Your personal sales
How many people you recruit
questions.w: Your team size is capped by how many people can run part of it without you, not how hard you work.

questions.q: Reliable, good for the room, turns up and gets results — most of a team is made of these. They are…
o: Glue
Core
High rollers
Match winners
questions.w: Core could run part of your team. High rollers are exceptional in the field. Glue holds the team together — and every team needs them.

questions.q: On the ten markers, there are three responses to feedback. Which is rare?
o: Applies
Defends
Accepts
Argues
questions.w: Defends, accepts, applies — only the third is rare. Watch what happens in the next two days.

questions.q: The three-step coaching flywheel for handing a job over is…
o: You do it, together, they do it
Tell, show, test
They do it, you review, you fix
Explain, delegate, check
questions.w: Hand a job over using the coaching flywheel — you do it, together, they do it.

questions.q: Which three checklist items should you start in week one, because they take months?
o: Develop a leader on a leader's team, hold four leaders for a month, score your team and revise a month later
Run the workshop, the tree pass and one-on-ones
The vehicle conversation, the placement plan and the battery fortnight
Both self-assessments and the question week
questions.w: These need calendar time you cannot compress. Start the slow ones first — everything else will fit around them.

questions.q: At what team size do most teams stall?
o: 5 to 8 — stretched, with too many calls
Up to 4 — when you know everyone
13 to 16 — managing leaders
17 to 20+ — second generation
questions.w: Your first core person has to start carrying people — this is where most teams stall permanently.

days.title: First Impressions · SEEC · Distance Theory

days.title: FAQs · Objection Handling Model
days.strap: Objections aren't obstacles — they're opportunities. Today you learn to love them.
